COMP Decoding Algorithm

Source: R/pp_decode.R
pp_comp.Rd

Decodes pooled test results using the Combinatorial Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (COMP) algorithm, which guarantees zero false negatives.

Usage

pp_comp(M, y, ct_threshold = 40)

Arguments

M

Binary pooling matrix \(\mathbf{M} \in \{0,1\}^{J \times N}\). It may be dense or sparse. Row \(j\) corresponds to pool \(\mathcal{P}_j\) and column \(i\) corresponds to individual \(i\).

y

Numeric vector of length \(J\) containing observed pool outcomes. Allowed inputs are either binary indicators \(Z_j \in \{0,1\}\) or quantitative Ct-like measurements encoded so that \(0\) means undetected and \(0 < y_j < \texttt{ct\_threshold}\) is treated as a positive pool.

ct_threshold

Numeric scalar giving the positivity threshold applied when y contains Ct-like values. The default is 40.

Value

A list with components:

candidates

Integer vector of potentially positive sample indices (1-indexed)

negatives

Integer vector of definitely negative sample indices

n_positive_pools

Integer; number of positive pools

Algorithm

For each sample \(j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}\):

$$\hat{x}_j = \begin{cases} 0 \text{ (negative)} & \text{if } \exists i : M_{ij} = 1 \land y_i = 0 \\ 1 \text{ (candidate)} & \text{if } \forall i : M_{ij} = 1 \Rightarrow y_i = 1 \end{cases}$$

In words: A sample is marked negative if it appears in ANY negative pool; it's a candidate (potentially positive) if ALL its pools are positive.

Theoretical Properties

  1. No false negatives: COMP never misses a true positive

  2. May have false positives: Negative samples in only positive pools are incorrectly marked as candidates

  3. Exact for PP designs: When \(k \leq k_{max}\), COMP is exact (no false positives) due to the intersection bound

Exactness Theorem for PP Matrices

For a PP matrix with parameters \((q, d, n_l)\):

If there are at most \(k_{max} = \lfloor(n_l-1)/(d-1)\rfloor\) true positives, COMP identifies them exactly.

Proof: Each negative sample shares at most \(d-1\) pools with each positive (intersection bound). With \(k\) positives, a negative shares at most \(k(d-1)\) pools. If \(n_l > k(d-1)\), at least one pool containing the negative is "clean" -> COMP marks it negative.

Time Complexity

\(O(m \times n)\) where \(m\) = pools, \(n\) = samples.

References

Chan, C. L., Che, P. H., Jaggi, S., & Saligrama, V. (2011). Non-adaptive probabilistic group testing with noisy measurements: Near-optimal bounds with efficient algorithms. 49th Annual Allerton Conference on Communication, Control, and Computing, 1832-1839.

Aldridge, M., Johnson, O., & Scarlett, J. (2019). Group testing: An information theory perspective. Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, 15(3-4), 196-392.

See also

pp_decode, pp_gpsr, pp_matrix

Other decoding: decoding_algorithms, pp_decode(), pp_gpsr(), pp_validate()

# P-BEST example
M <- pp_matrix(q = 8, d = 3, nl = 6, N = 384)
